components.text: Whether diverse biblical genres require evaluation according to the purpose and standards appropriate to each genre.
Whether incidental anachronisms or rearranged events necessarily defeat the deeper intended truth of a historical work.
Whether biblical claims must be assessed according to the genre and purpose of each text.
Whether concrete Gospel discrepancies should be treated as reliability-defeating contradictions under ancient historical standards.
Whether non-eyewitness collection of testimony and human transmission can nevertheless produce reliable ancient history.
Whether nonidentical details and non-eyewitness collection defeat the Gospels' historical reliability.
Whether documented editing and possible oral alteration materially weaken Gospel transmission reliability.
Whether nonidentical Gospel accounts should be weighed cumulatively or rejected because of their differing details.
Whether features of the received narratives provide affirmative authenticity despite evidence of editing and transmission.
Whether nonidentical Gospel accounts should cumulatively support or instead weaken historical reliability.
Whether known textual editing and plausible oral alteration undermine the accounts' evidential value.
Whether Genesis may count as scientifically informative when favorable while being treated as non-scientific when its ordering conflicts with observation.
Whether Genesis may count as scientific evidence when favorable while contrary scientific details are excluded.
Whether favorable and unfavorable evidence are treated under a consistent rule when inferring biblical reliability.
Whether mundane archaeological corroboration answers evidence of textual alteration or establishes central Gospel events.
Whether favorable and unfavorable evidence are treated by a consistent inferential standard.
Whether matters beyond ordinary reason or natural expectation supply evidence for specifically biblical miraculous claims.
Whether the possibility of resurrection adds evidential weight to testimonial reports that it occurred.
Whether reason's limits or theological possibility provide evidence for specifically biblical extraordinary claims.
Whether mundane archaeological corroboration supplies evidence for particular biblical miracle reports.
Whether later Christian moral development can reconcile morally troubling Old Testament practices with biblical moral authority.
Whether Old Testament violence defeats biblical moral truth despite later New Testament teaching.
Whether later moral development or fulfillment resolves the moral status of earlier divine commands to kill noncombatants.
Whether later moral development can preserve authority without justifying earlier divine commands to kill noncombatants.
Whether later Christian restraints explain or justify the earlier divine command to kill women and children.
Whether the conquest commands themselves are compatible with divine moral authority.
Why later Christian restraints resolve the moral status of earlier divinely ordered noncombatant killing.
Whether later Christian moral restraint establishes the adequacy of biblical moral development in the face of specific harmful laws.
Whether incremental moral development adequately explains the Bible's failure to require humane treatment of enslaved families.
Whether later Christian moral restraints answer distinct defects in biblical slave law.
Why biblical slave law omitted the simple reform of releasing a freed man's wife and children with him.
Why biblical law omitted the simple reform of preserving an enslaved family upon the man's release.
Whether the significance of Exodus should be fixed exclusively by oppressive legal content despite its established liberatory reception.
Whether later beneficial use can alter the moral status of an earlier troubling command.
Whether reception can answer the specific moral defects and omissions contained in biblical slave law.
Whether Christian abolitionist reception shows that the Bible itself presents a coherent anti-slavery moral direction.
Whether liberatory communal use outweighs contrary Old and New Testament teachings concerning slavery.
Whether liberating reception resolves contrary scriptural approval and obedience instructions concerning slavery.
Whether abolitionist Christian use establishes coherent biblical opposition to slavery.
